passage:
Dear Diary, Friday night
Ayesha invited me to her family's iftar today. Watching them wait for the azaan, so quiet and sure, I realised I've never once asked myself why I do puja with Amma every morning. I just do it. On the walk home Ayesha said she's been reading about her faith on her own, not just what her Nani tells her, and there are parts she's still arguing with. That hit me. So tonight I made two lists: things I believe because I've thought about them, and things I just inherited. The second list was longer. I think I'm keeping the morning diya, but for my own reason: it's the one quiet minute I get with Amma. The rest I want to read about properly.
Aparna

qa.q: Where did Ayesha invite Aparna today?
qa.a: To her family's iftar.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel on seeing that the second list was longer?
qa.a: Aparna felt unsettled but curious, seeing how much had been inherited rather than chosen.

qa.q: What is a thoughtful next step for Aparna's exploration?
qa.a: Aparna could read about these beliefs properly and talk them over with Amma, keeping what feels true while staying respectful.

qa.q: How does Ayesha describe her own relationship with her faith?
qa.a: Ayesha is reading about her faith independently and still arguing with some parts, so for Ayesha belief is something actively thought through.

grounding: Shows a teenager starting to examine inherited religious practice and choosing which parts to keep for personal reasons.

passage: Mridul, you keep asking your Deepika Bua how she ended up designing bridges. At sixteen I was sure I'd be a doctor, because my father and everyone at the dinner table said so. That summer I volunteered at the clinic in our town and fainted at the first blood test I watched. I cried the whole way home. My friend Salma dragged me to the river instead, and I spent the afternoon asking why the old railway bridge hadn't fallen in the floods. That night I made two columns: things I'm good at, and things I love. Maths and drawing were in both. Blood was in neither. I told my father the next week. He was quiet for a long time, then asked to see my drawings.

qa.q: Where did Deepika volunteer that summer?
qa.a: At the clinic in her town.

qa.q: How did young Deepika feel after fainting at the blood test?
qa.a: She felt upset and shaken, crying all the way home, as her planned future suddenly seemed wrong.

qa.q: What turning point helped Deepika choose a new path?
qa.a: Making two columns, what she was good at and what she loved, showed maths and drawing in both and pointed her away from medicine.

qa.q: How might Deepika's father have felt when she told him?
qa.a: He was quiet for a long time, perhaps disappointed or surprised, but asking to see her drawings suggests he was willing to understand.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager testing an expected career against her real strengths and interests, told by an aunt.

passage: On the metro home from coaching class in Delhi, Zubin was quiet. Usually Amandeep filled silences with jokes, and usually Zubin laughed. Today Zubin said, "My parents are separating. Dad's moving out on Sunday." Amandeep opened his mouth to crack something, anything, then shut it. He thought of his cousin Harjot, who always just sat with him when things went wrong at home, and how much that had mattered. "I'll come over Sunday," Amandeep said. "We don't have to talk. I'll bring the chess set." Zubin nodded, eyes on the window. That night Amandeep typed into his phone notes: Be the friend who shows up. Less joking, more staying.

qa.q: When is Zubin's dad moving out?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep shut his mouth instead of cracking a joke?
qa.a: He felt concerned for Zubin and sensed a joke would be wrong, remembering how much quiet support had comforted him.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do on Sunday to live out his note?
qa.a: He could turn up as promised, play chess, and let Zubin decide whether to talk.

qa.q: What might Amandeep's offer mean to Zubin?
qa.a: Zubin probably feels less alone, knowing a friend will be there on a hard day without pressure to talk.

grounding: Shows a teenager deciding what kind of friend he wants to be when a friend is going through a hard time.

passage: The school trip bus to Jaipur was leaving in five minutes, and Kashish still hadn't picked a seat. The back rows belonged to Tanya's group; everyone knew that without being told. The middle was the quiz-club crowd, where Kunal waved her over to the empty seat beside him. Kashish had been at Tanya's sleepover last week and in quiz club since Class 8. Tanya called, "Kash, we saved you one!" The teacher shouted, "Sit anywhere, now!" Kashish felt both groups watching. She sat with Kunal, then turned and said to Tanya, "Swap at the lunch stop?" Tanya shrugged, lips tight. Kunal handed her an earphone. "Quiz on the way?"

qa.q: Where was the school trip bus going?
qa.a: To Jaipur.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling as both groups watched her?
qa.a: She felt torn and under pressure, belonging partly to both groups and worried about upsetting either.

qa.q: How did Kashish try to handle the group boundaries?
qa.a: She sat with Kunal but offered Tanya a swap at the lunch stop, trying to stay close to both groups without snubbing either.

qa.q: How might Tanya see Kashish's choice?
qa.a: Tanya seems a little hurt or annoyed, taking the seat as a sign of which group Kashish really belongs to.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager caught between two groups with firm, unspoken seating boundaries under time pressure.

passage: Okay, Gurleen, you want the whole embarrassing story from Simran herself? Fine. In Class 10, everyone who mattered had those chunky white sneakers. I didn't even like them. But I saved my birthday money, bought a pair, and wore them on the first day of term like a trophy. I got exactly two comments. Then the group started ending every sentence with the same slang word, so I did that too. I laughed at jokes I didn't find funny. By Diwali I was sitting at their table, and I felt... tired. Like I was wearing someone else's face. The day I switched back to my old canvas shoes, you were the only one who noticed. You said, "There you are." I still think about that.

qa.q: How many comments did Simran get on the sneakers?
qa.a: Exactly two comments.

qa.q: How did Simran feel sitting at the group's table by Diwali?
qa.a: She felt tired and hollow, as if she were wearing someone else's face.

qa.q: What might Simran do differently if a new trend appears?
qa.a: She could ask herself whether she actually likes it or just wants the group's approval, and choose on that basis.

qa.q: What is it like for Gurleen to notice the old canvas shoes?
qa.a: Gurleen seems glad and relieved to see the real Simran again, saying, "There you are." 🤍

grounding: Shows a teenager copying trends to climb socially and finding it empty.

passage: I'm Pankaj, in Himani's section. On Thursday the class group decided on a mass bunk for Friday's last two periods, to go and see a film. Everyone reacted with thumbs-ups. Himani didn't reply for an hour. Then she wrote, "I've got band practice, you guys go." Someone replied "boring 🙄" and a couple of people laughed at it. At lunch on Friday I saw her sitting a bit apart, fiddling with her drumsticks, not really eating. But when the bell rang, she walked to the music room, not the gate. I went with the others. I don't know if she regretted it. She was smiling when I passed the music room window, though.

qa.q: What reason did Himani give for not joining the bunk?
qa.a: She had band practice.

qa.q: What does Himani fiddling with her drumsticks at lunch suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy and a little left out after the "boring" comment, even though she had decided.

qa.q: What could help Himani hold her choice without feeling isolated?
qa.a: She could spend time with band friends who share her interest, and remind herself why practice matters to her.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Himani's choice?
qa.a: Pankaj notices her unease but also her smile, unsure whether she regretted it, while going along with the others.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager choosing her own commitment over a class bunk despite teasing, seen by a classmate.

passage:
Subject: About yesterday's feedback
Hi Afreen,
I've been thinking about what you said after rehearsal: that my slides had too much text and I kept talking over Nandini. Honestly, my first reaction was to snap back, and I'm sorry I muttered "fine, do it yourself." That wasn't fair.
I went through the slides again last night. You're right: slide 4 had eleven lines. I've cut every slide to three points and moved the rest to my notes. I didn't notice I was talking over Nandini, so could you tap the table if it happens on Friday?
One thing I'd gently push back on: I think the conclusion needs the data chart, not just the quote. Can we try both versions tomorrow?
Anirban

qa.q: How many lines did slide 4 have?
qa.a: Slide 4 had eleven lines.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel at first when Afreen gave feedback?
qa.a: Anirban felt defensive and irritated, wanting to snap back, which led to the muttered "fine, do it yourself."

qa.q: What makes Anirban's email a good way to handle the conflict?
qa.a: It apologises for the snap, acts on the fair points, asks for a signal about talking over Nandini, and raises the one disagreement politely with a way to test both versions.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel reading this email?
qa.a: Afreen would likely feel respected and relieved that the feedback was heard, and more open to Anirban's point about the chart. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager taking a project partner's criticism without defensiveness and raising a disagreement diplomatically.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday
Lalremsiami came in at lunch with her friend Shreya, who said, "She hasn't been sleeping." Lalremsiami said she keeps reading about floods and heatwaves at night and wonders why she should plan for college "when everything might be underwater by then." She said it angrily, then went quiet and pressed her palms into her eyes. She also said she's scared she'll never be good enough to fix anything. I didn't argue with her fears. I listened, said it sounds heavy to carry, and asked what small thing feels in her control. She mentioned the school garden club. We agreed she'll try one session, keep news reading out of bedtime, and meet me again Monday. With her agreement, I'm calling her mother today.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami keep reading about at night?
qa.a: Floods and heatwaves.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she pressed her palms into her eyes?
qa.a: She seemed overwhelmed, a mix of anger, fear and dread about the future and her place in it.

qa.q: What did the counsellor's approach get right?
qa.a: The counsellor listened without arguing, named how heavy it felt, found one small step in her control, and arranged follow-up and support at home.

qa.q: What is it like for Shreya to bring Lalremsiami in?
qa.a: Shreya is clearly worried about a friend who isn't sleeping and cares enough to walk Lalremsiami to the counsellor.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's general dread and frustration about the world's future and a counsellor's calm response.

passage: Afreen, beti, you asked why your old Divyansh Uncle from accounts spends every weekend at the lake. When I was fifteen, the lake behind our Bhopal colony was turning into a dump. One morning I found a heron tangled in a plastic net, and I couldn't stop thinking about it. I started counting birds every dawn before school, in a notebook with a torn cover. I wrote to the municipal office, got no answer, and wrote again. I dragged my friend Qadir to clean the bank every Sunday for a year. My marks slipped that term, and my mother was furious. But when the corporation finally put up a fence and bins, I cried on the bank like a fool. I still have that notebook: 812 herons counted.

qa.q: What did young Divyansh find tangled in a plastic net?
qa.a: A heron.

qa.q: How did young Divyansh feel when the corporation put up the fence and bins?
qa.a: Divyansh felt overwhelmed with relief and joy, crying on the bank after a year of effort.

qa.q: Which choice kept the lake campaign alive after the first letter got no answer?
qa.a: Writing again and cleaning the bank every Sunday for a year kept the pressure on, even when nothing seemed to change.

qa.q: How did Divyansh's mother see the lake work that term?
qa.a: Divyansh's mother was furious when the marks slipped, seeing the lake work as a distraction from school.

grounding: Shows a teenager's intense, lasting drive to protect a lake, told by a senior colleague as a memory.

passage: You want to know why I acted like I didn't care, Alka? It's Jeevan you're talking to; you know I care about everything. When the state team list came out and my name wasn't on it, I shrugged in front of everyone. "Football's just a hobby," I said. I stopped going to practice, told people I was busy, even laughed when Coach asked where I'd been. Inside, it felt like someone had switched off a light. It was easier to say "whatever" than to admit I'd trained two years for that list. The day you found my old boots in the bin and fished them out without a word, I nearly broke. I'm back at practice now. It still hurts, but less than pretending did.

qa.q: Where did Alka find Jeevan's old boots?
qa.a: In the bin.

qa.q: What was Jeevan really feeling while saying "Football's just a hobby"?
qa.a: Jeevan felt crushed and hurt, as if a light had been switched off, and the shrug hid that pain.

qa.q: What might have helped Jeevan sooner than pretending?
qa.a: Admitting the disappointment to a friend or to Coach early could have let Jeevan face the setback and return to practice sooner.

qa.q: What is it like for Alka to watch Jeevan act as if nothing matters?
qa.a: Alka likely sees through it and worries, which is why Alka quietly fishes the boots out of the bin.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager faking indifference to hide the hurt of missing a team selection.
